# Order {#sec-order}

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes & Chapter summary"}

1. **Explain** how connecting observations makes their grouping and order easier to see.

2. **Distinguish** grouping observations into a series from ordering the observations within that series.

3. **Use** lines to display change over time, and **compare** line and area charts for ordered data.

4. **Explain** how stacking changes the interpretation of a chart and when a shared baseline is more useful.

:::

## Why order matters

In @sec-groups, we learned how to distinguish groups of observations.
Now we will look at observations that also have a meaningful order,
such as time of day or an increasing dose of a treatment.
In the following exercise,
we will see how the grouping strategies we learned previously
can be effectively complemented
when working with ordered data.

::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

In the chart below,
we can see how CO₂ emissions per capita have changed over time
for the world's continents.
As you can see,
the chart applies the strategies we have learned so far
and uses color to group observations from different continents.
But the overlap between the different groups
makes it difficult to follow changes over time
for any particular continent, and the chart is a bit confusing
even after studying it for a while.
How do you think you could change this chart
to make it easier to see how CO₂ emissions per capita
for each continent have changed over time?


```{python setup}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd
from utils import show_df
```

```{python bad-points}
#| echo: false
years = range(1850, 2030, 8)
co2_per_capita = pd.read_csv('data/co-emissions-per-capita.csv').query('Year.isin(@years)')
points = alt.Chart(co2_per_capita, width=400).mark_point().encode(
    x=alt.X('Year').axis(format='d').scale(zero=False),
    y=alt.Y('CO2_emissions_per_capita').title('Tonnes of CO2 per capita'),
    color=alt.Color('Entity').title(None)
)

points
```

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

Do you think connecting the points belonging to the same continent
would make it easier or harder to spot trends?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

We can use the natural order of the observations
to connect the points that belong to the same continent with a line.
Drawing a line from the earliest to the most recent year
helps us with two things:
it makes it easier to see changes over time for any single continent,
and it makes it easier to see which points belong to which continent.
As such,
a line is a graphical tool that assists with both ordering and grouping.

```{python line-overlay}
points.mark_line() + points.mark_point(filled=True, strokeOpacity=1)
```

:::::

::::

:::


## Using lines to order and group data

To explore how to create line charts,
we will visualize population and fertility estimates at eight-year intervals from 1850 to 2018.
The data comes from the [Gapminder country-level dataset](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joelostblom/teaching-datasets/main/world-data-gapminder.csv),
and has been adapted for this textbook.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: order-data-preparation-notes
#| echo: false
# years = range(1850, 2030, 8)
# world = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_world_trends.csv').query('year.isin(@years)').to_csv('data/gapminder_world_from_1850.csv', index=False)
# regions = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_region_trends.csv').query('year.isin(@years)').to_csv('data/gapminder_regions_from_1850.csv', index=False)
```

```{python}
#| label: read-data-python
#| output: false
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

world = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_world_from_1850.csv')
world
```

```{python}
#| label: show-regions-python
#| echo: false
show_df(world)
```

### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: order-table-setup
#| include: false
source("utils.R")
```

```{r}
#| label: read-data-r
#| output: false
library(tidyverse)

world <- read_csv('data/gapminder_world_from_1850.csv')
world
```

```{r}
#| label: show-regions-r
#| echo: false
show_df(world)
```

:::
When reading in a new dataset,
it is always a good idea to have a look at a few rows
as we did above,
to get an idea of what the data looks like.

The world dataset has one row per sampled year,
with the total population of the countries in the source dataset
and the average of their fertility estimates (`children_per_woman`).
Fertility here estimates the number of children a woman would have over her lifetime
if the year's age-specific birth rates persisted; it is not the number born per woman in a single year.
Each country contributes equally to the average in our table,
so this is a country average rather than a population-weighted global estimate.
The regional dataset, which we will use later, applies the same summaries within each region.

Since the data reaches all the way back to the 1850s,
it would be really interesting to plot
how the world population grew over the period covered by the data.
We can use a line plot to show this change over time.

::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

Sketch the visualization
(by hand is better than in your mind, which is better than nothing...)
so that it is clear what you expect the plot to look like
before continuing.

:::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

If we sketched this visualization on paper,
we might expect something like this:
a single line that rises from the 1800s to the end of our dataset
as the population increases.

![Drawing of estimated world population growth](https://viz-learn.mds.ubc.ca/module2/drawing.png){#drawing}

::::
:::

Now we are ready to create our plot!
By convention,
time variables such as `year`
tend to be laid out along the x-axis,
while quantitative measures such as `population`
tend to occupy the y-axis.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

In Altair,
we use `mark_line()`
to connect observations with a line.

```{python}
#| label: population-line-alt
alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x='year',
    y='population'
)
```

You can see that the formatting on the x-axis
includes a comma as a thousands separator.
While this is desirable for regular quantitative variables,
it is not how we are used to seeing years displayed.
To deal with this,
we can either change the underlying data type
or the number formatting of the axis.

To change the axis formatting,
we need to leverage the helper class `alt.X`
(similar helpers exist for other channels,
such as `alt.Y` and `alt.Color`).
These classes help us customize many aspects of our charts.
When using just `x='year'`,
we're using shorthand for `alt.X('year')`;
we just save ourselves some typing.

Here we are going to set `alt.X('year').axis(format='d')`,
where the `d` is short for "decimal integer"
(i.e., a base-10 integer).

```{python}
#| label: population-line-alt-format
alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='population'
)
```

Now the years are formatted as we are used to seeing them!

### ggplot

In ggplot,
we use `geom_line()`
to connect observations with a line.

```{r}
#| label: population-line-gg
ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
    geom_line()
```

:::

::: {.column-margin}

<br><br>
**Population plateau**

Although the historical curve might suggest that the population
will keep growing rapidly,
[the UN's 2024 projections suggest a peak of around 10.3 billion people
before the end of the century, followed by a gradual decline](https://ourworldindata.org/world-population-growth-past-future).

:::

Interestingly,
the line in this example helps us notice a change in the slope.
The world population increased
more slowly in absolute numbers before around 1950,
and more rapidly afterwards.

After making any chart,
it's beneficial to ask yourself:
"Is this what I expected to see from the data?"
and "Does what I'm seeing make sense with what I know about this topic?"
If we think about what happened in the world
around the time of the change in the population growth dynamics,
a major event that stands out was the end of World War II in 1945.
It seems reasonable that transitioning from a war
involving many countries around the world
to a time of peace and increased safety
could lead to an increase in the number of babies born.
Let's explore whether the timing of the change coincides with an increase
in our country-average fertility measure.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: children_per_woman-line-alt
alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='children_per_woman'
)
```

### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: children_per_woman-line-gg
ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = children_per_woman)) +
    geom_line()
```

:::

The country-average fertility estimate does show a rise
from the late 1930s to the early 1960s, followed by a decline.
This "explosion" is what is commonly referred to as the "baby boom".
However, remember that this chart averages country-level fertility estimates
rather than taking the population into each country into account,
so it does not directly show the total number of babies born in the world.

::: {.callout-default .deep-dive}

One more important piece of the puzzle here
would be to look at life expectancy data
to see if people were also living longer lives
during this period,
which would also contribute to population growth.
Historical life expectancy estimates vary in coverage and reliability,
but you can [explore available estimates at Our World in Data
](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/life-expectancy?time=1900..latest&country=OWID_WRL~Americas~OWID_EUR~OWID_AFR~OWID_ASI).

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid claiming causation from visualizations alone

You might have heard that "correlation is not causation",
and that applies here too.
Although the end of World War II
seems like a plausible contributor to some of the trends we have explored,
it is important to understand
that plausibility alone does not establish the cause
of the observed patterns.
Usually, several contributing factors interact
to produce a more complex picture.
[This article about the baby boom
](https://ourworldindata.org/baby-boom-seven-charts)
elaborates on what we explored here.
Among other things,
it notes that many countries
saw birth rates begin to rise
even before World War II.

:::

## Combining lines and points

Generally,
it is helpful
to add points on top of a line
to indicate exactly where each observation from the data lies.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

In Altair,
we combine lines and points
through a concept called layering,
where charts are superimposed on each other.
The `+` operator means to "layer"
a chart on top of another chart.
<!-- TODO (it's also possible to use `alt.layer(...)` -->
<!-- with a list of charts). -->

```{python}
#| label: population-line-points-alt
line = alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='children_per_woman'
)
line + line.mark_point(filled=True)
```

Each basic Altair chart specification uses a single mark type,
so `line.mark_point()` *replaces* the line mark with a point mark
in the chart that we are layering on top of our original.
<!-- TODO consider base.line + base.point? -->

### ggplot

In ggplot,
we combine lines and points
through a concept called layering,
where charts (or "graphical layers") are superimposed on each other.
The `+` operator means to "layer"
a geom on top of another geom.

```{r}
#| label: population-line-points-gg
ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = children_per_woman)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point()
```

:::

This highlights something important:
what does the line between the data points mean?
Let's find out in the next exercise.


::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

In our data,
there are only observations from every eighth year,
but the line we have drawn is continuous
and has a defined value for `children_per_woman`
even between the points in the chart.
For example,
in this zoomed-in view
we can see that the line at the year 1950
suggests a country-average fertility estimate of approximately 5.4 children per woman.
But as we can see from the points in the chart,
our data does not contain any observation from exactly the year 1950.
What conclusions can we draw
about the fertility estimate for this year?

```{python}
#| label: population-line-points-zoom
#| echo: false
line = alt.Chart(world.query('year > 1920')).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y=alt.Y('children_per_woman').scale(domain=(2.5, 6))
)
line + line.mark_point(filled=True)
```

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

Think about the purpose of the line:
is it just a visual aid,
or does it represent any feature of the underlying data?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

The line segments between two observations are there to guide the eye;
they do not establish what the values are
at every unobserved moment between two points.
Although the line is a simple linear interpolation between observations,
which might seem harmless,
it is important to consider whether the distance between two points
represents a long enough period
that important changes could be hidden by a straight line.
To understand this more deeply,
we can look at what would happen if the observations were closer
or farther apart in time,
as in the chart below.

```{python}
#| label: population-line-points-zoom2
#| echo: false
years = range(1926, 2010, 2)
world2 = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_world_trends.csv').query('year.isin(@years)')
title = 'Every 2nd year'
line = alt.Chart(world2, title=title, height=220, width=220).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y=alt.Y('children_per_woman').scale(domain=(2.5, 6))
)
every_2nd_year = line + line.mark_point(filled=True)

years = range(1928, 2030, 20)
title = 'Every 20th year'
line = alt.Chart(world2.query('year.isin(@years)'), title=title, height=220, width=220).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y=alt.Y('children_per_woman').scale(domain=(2.5, 6))
)
every_20th_year = line + line.mark_point(filled=True)
alt.concat(every_2nd_year, every_20th_year)
```

As you can see,
drawing a line between the observations sampled 20 years apart
misses the rise in the average fertility estimate:
it decreased until around 1940,
then increased until around 1960,
after which it started to decrease again.

How closely observations need to be spaced
for straight connecting lines to be a useful approximation
depends on which question we are asking.
For example,
if we are interested in exploring seasonal variation within each year,
then even a chart with one observation every year
would be insufficient. We would need more frequent observations,
such as monthly values.

:::::
::::
:::

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid connecting unordered categories with a line

As we just saw,
we need to be careful when interpreting a line between two observations
along a quantitative axis.
For the same reason,
we should generally avoid using a line
to connect observations along an axis of unordered categories.
Here are two representations of the same population values:

```{python}
#| label: population-line-categorical
#| echo: false
regions = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_regions_from_1850.csv')

points = alt.Chart(
    regions.query('year==2018 & region.isin(["Africa", "Americas", "Europe"])'),
    height=250,
    width=alt.Step(60)
).mark_point(size=60, filled=True, color='#FF0039').encode(
    x=alt.X('region').title(None).sort(['Africa', 'Europe', 'Americas']),
    y=alt.Y('sum(population)')
        .scale(domain=(00_000_000, 1_350_000_000))
        .axis(labelExpr="format(datum.value / 1e6, ',.0f')")
        .title('Population in 2018 (millions)')
)
points | points.mark_line(color='#FF0039') + points
```

The chart to the left is easy to interpret;
it shows how many people lived on each continent in 2018,
with a point for each continent's value.
But what about the line chart to the right?
What does it mean that the line is at 1,000 million as it goes from Africa to Europe?
That 1,000 million people lived somewhere between Europe and Africa?
No,
in contrast to how a line connecting two quantitative values
can hint at what the value between them *might* have been,
there is no meaningful numerical interval between these unordered categories,
and therefore lines should generally not be used
to connect observations across them.

:::

::: {.callout-default .deep-dive}

Sometimes we want to show how the relationship between two quantitative
variables has changed over time.
We can do this by plotting the two variables of interest on the x- and y-axes,
then connecting the points in chronological order.

:::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

The `order` encoding controls
the order in which observations will be connected by a line.
Since there is no visible axis for the year,
it would be difficult to know in which direction to read the chart;
is the most recent year represented by the point in the top-left or bottom-right corner?
To avoid this confusion, we add a tooltip
so that you can see which year each point corresponds to
when hovering over it with the mouse pointer.

```{python}
#| label: line-order-2d-alt
line = alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x='children_per_woman',
    y='population',
    order='year',
    # Display the numeric year as an integer without a thousands separator
    tooltip=alt.Tooltip('year', format='d')
)
line + line.mark_point(filled=True)
```

### ggplot

By default, `geom_line()` connects points
in the order of the variable on the x-axis.
To connect points in another order,
we can use `geom_path()` instead.
This geom connects observations in dataframe row order,
so we need to make sure our data is sorted by the variable
we want the connection order to represent.

Since there is no visible axis for the year,
it would be difficult to know in which direction to read the chart;
is the most recent year represented by the point in the top-left or bottom-right corner?
To avoid this confusion, we add a text label
so that you can identify the earliest
and most recent observations.

```{r}
#| label: line-order-2d-gg
endpoints <- world |>
  filter(year %in% range(year, na.rm = TRUE))
ggplot(world |> arrange(year), aes(x = children_per_woman, y = population, label = year)) +
    geom_path() +
    geom_point() +
    geom_text(
        data = endpoints,
        vjust = -0.5  # Move the labels above the points to avoid overlap
    )
```

::::

So how do we read this chart?
We start by finding the year corresponding to the earliest observation;
in this case, it is at the bottom right of the chart.
Then we can follow the progression of the relationship between
the world's population and the country-average fertility estimate
over time (i.e. towards the top left corner).
The horizontal space between two points
corresponds to the change in the country-average fertility estimate,
whereas the vertical space corresponds to the change in the world population
between those two years.
If the points are close together,
the changes were small relative to the displayed axis scales;
points farther apart indicate larger changes on those scales.

:::

## Areas and multiple ordered groups

Another way of representing ordered data
is to fill the area between a line and a baseline.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: population-area-alt
alt.Chart(world).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='population'
)
```

### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: population-area-gg
ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
    geom_area()
```

:::

Both lines and areas preserve the sequence of values over time.
Filling the area down to a zero baseline emphasizes the magnitude of those values,
while a line emphasizes the path through them.
When displaying multiple ordered groups,
lines and areas have different advantages,
which we will learn about in this exercise.


::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

We now use the `regions` dataframe,
which contains a separate population value
for each region in each year.
Region determines which observations belong to the same group,
and year determines their order within that group.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

Setting `color` applies to both areas and lines;
if we wanted to control them individually,
we could instead use `stroke` (for lines)
and `fill` (for areas).
Here we also use the `|` layout operator
to position the plots next to each other horizontally
(`&` lays them out vertically instead;
we will learn more about layouts in a later chapter).

```{python}
#| label: population-stacked-alt
regions = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_regions_from_1850.csv')

base = alt.Chart(regions, width=150, height=150).encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='population',
    color='region'
)
base.mark_area() | base.mark_line()
```

### ggplot

`geom_area()` stacks the regional areas by default.
The population values are already in the dataset,
so we can map them directly to the y-axis.
To set the area color, we use the `fill` aesthetic,
whereas the line color is controlled by the `color` aesthetic.
We map both to `region`.
<!-- TODO Should we set these in the geoms? That introduces several new concepts, but avoids creating an outline for each area. -->
Here we also use the `|` layout operator from the `patchwork` library
to position the plots next to each other horizontally
(`/` lays them out vertically instead;
we will learn more about layouts in a later chapter).

```{r}
#| label: population-stacked-gg
#| fig-width: 8
#| message: false
library(patchwork)

regions <- read_csv('data/gapminder_regions_from_1850.csv')

base <- ggplot(regions, aes(x = year, y = population, fill = region, color = region))
base + geom_area(show.legend = FALSE) | base + geom_line()
```

:::

For each of these three questions,
which chart is most appropriate?

1. How has the world population changed over time?
2. How has the population of the Americas changed over time?
3. Which region had the second-highest population in 2018?

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

Note how the areas are stacked on top of each other,
whereas the lines are not.
Which chart makes the total easiest to read?
Which lets you compare regional values against a shared baseline?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

1. The area chart makes it easiest
   to see how the total world population has changed over time,
   as we can read this value directly off the y-axis
   since the areas are stacked on top of each other.
2. Using a line chart is the preferred choice
   when we want to focus on comparing groups,
   either exact individual observations or the progression over time,
   rather than the total of the groups added together.
   From the stacked colored regions,
   we also get a rough idea of how each region has grown,
   but it is hard to make exact comparisons,
   because most regions do not share a baseline.
   The drawback of a line chart is that
   it's quite cognitively demanding
   to try to reconstruct the total world population
   by adding all the lines up together,
   especially over time!
3. For the same reasons as in (2),
   a line chart makes it easier to see that Africa had the second-highest population in 2018,
   behind Asia. The sampled values show Africa below the Americas in 1994
   and above it in 2002.

:::::

::::

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid layering areas and stacking lines

While it might initially seem that overlapping areas instead of stacking them
could remedy some of the issues mentioned above,
the filled regions can obscure one another,
as you can see below
(there are a few exceptions such as density plots
which we will see in a later chapter).

```{python}
#| label: fertility-overlapping
#| echo: false
alt.Chart(regions).mark_area(opacity=0.4).encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y=alt.Y('children_per_woman').stack(False),
    color='region'
)
```

Similarly,
stacked lines are usually difficult to interpret:
each line's height represents a cumulative sum rather than its own group's value.
If the sum is meaningful,
use an area chart instead.

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid stacking areas when summing groups is nonsensical

Avoid stacked area charts when
the sum of the different groups in the chart is not meaningful,
since stacking effectively sums the area heights together.
For example,
if we wanted to know the average number of children per woman around the world,
stacking areas does not make sense
since this adds the regional averages rather than calculating an overall average.
Reading the y-axis of the stacked areas thus becomes
misleading and confusing;
the world average wasn't 30 children per woman in the 1800s...

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fertility-stacked
alt.Chart(regions).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='children_per_woman',
    color='region'
)
```

:::
